source.title: Neuroplasticity and Corruption in Model Mechanisms: A Case Study Of Indirect Object Identification
source.authors: V. Chhabra; Ding Zhu; M. Khalili

page_placements.theme: Training decides which heads carry suppressive roles and how strongly

record.tranche_reason: It studies IOI circuit mechanisms and self-repair in GPT-2-small using task-specific fine-tuning and circuit analysis, rather than reproducing the original copy-suppression measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Copy Suppression and characterizes negative name movers as copy-suppressor heads, but does not test L10H7, measure the 76.9% loss contribution, or directly measure ordinary-text copy suppression. The relevant original-work result is the reported self-repair trend for head 9.9 and the reported amplification of negative name-mover heads. The corrupted-dataset results are intentionally induced task behavior and are not treated as evidence of ordinary behavior.
record.test_reason: The paper takes from McDougall et al. that negative name movers are copy-suppressor heads and uses that framing to interpret its fine-tuning results. It never measures copy suppression itself: there is no test of L10H7, no check of whether suppression targets tokens both predicted and present in context, and no separation of copy suppression's share of self-repair. Its self-repair metric for L9H9 measures total compensation, and its negative-name-mover results are logit attributions under task fine-tuning. Neither can confirm or refute any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that task-specific fine-tuning amplifies existing circuit mechanisms, including negative name movers, and that toxic fine-tuning corrupts localized components. They also conclude that models show neuroplasticity when retrained on clean data. Their self-repair result is a preliminary appendix finding that self-repair for L9H9 increases with fine-tuning, which they hypothesize comes from more backup name movers and dropout. They call negative name movers copy suppressors only by citing McDougall et al.
record.recipe_differences: Uses IOI circuit discovery, task-specific fine-tuning, head attribution, and a self-repair metric; it does not reproduce the original study's comprehensive L10H7 QK/OV and loss-contribution analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Self-repair capacity varies over training: the text reports an early increase followed by a phase shift.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-repair after ablating name mover L9H9 increases roughly linearly over clean-IOI fine-tuning, then shifts phase (Fig. 13). It is attributed hypothetically to backup name movers and dropout.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-specific fine-tuning increases total self-repair for ablated copier heads in the IOI circuit.

fits_no_version.finding: Negative name-mover heads keep and amplify their negative logit attribution under clean-IOI fine-tuning rather than disappearing (Fig. 4a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning on a task amplifies negative heads that work against the task.

fits_no_version.finding: After fine-tuning on Subject Duplication, negative name movers switch to suppressing S, mirroring the name movers' new output (Figs. 9-10). This is behaviour induced by corrupted training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Negative name movers track and invert whatever the name movers copy, even after retraining.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (NAACL), 2025
record.problems: The claim-relevant self-repair trend is presented as a figure without numerical values or uncertainty. The study does not directly test the L10H7 copy-suppression mechanism or isolate the causal self-repair pathway.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results directly measure the listed claim versions. The corrupted-dataset findings intentionally induce changed task behavior and are not evidence about naturally occurring copy suppression.

untested.parts: Not tested: L10H7's role on the training distribution.
Not tested: QK/OV analysis of the suppression mechanism and its share of the loss effect.
Not tested: whether copy suppression contributes to self-repair when an upstream copier is ablated. Only total self-repair is measured.
Not tested: whether negative name movers or other heads implement copy suppression. Other models and sizes are not studied.
Not tested: the split of self-repair across mechanisms.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and its 'supports' labels for V4 and V5 are not warranted: both rows measure constructs other than copy suppression. The text loosely conflates 'Copy Suppressor Heads, i.e, Name Mover Heads' in Appendix D. The original source is cited (McDougall et al. 2023).

versions.untested_parts: Does not test L10H7, token-level copying suppression, or whether the role dominates across the training distribution.
Does not analyze L10H7's QK/OV circuits or quantify their contribution to loss.
Does not measure calibration or overconfidence in copying.

Measures self-repair behavior for head 9.9 over fine-tuning, but does not establish the specific causal pathway that upstream-copy ablation leaves less to suppress or quantify copy suppression's share of compensation.
Examines negative name-mover mechanisms in the IOI task, but does not directly demonstrate the matching-token copy-suppression behavior on ordinary text or test other models and sizes.
Does not compare copy suppression with other mechanisms as shares of self-repair across a distribution.

rows.note: The authors identify the investigated heads as copy-suppressor heads/name movers, but the plot and discussion do not isolate the proposed upstream-copier-ablation pathway.
rows.check: Measures total self-repair after ablating L9H9, a name mover rather than a copy suppressor, across clean-IOI fine-tuning epochs. The metric does not attribute the compensation to copy suppression. The authors hypothesize dropout and extra backup name movers as the cause. It cannot bear on V4, which is about copy suppression's role in self-repair. The value is figure only (Fig. 13, about 1.6 to 2.8).

relation.reason: Section 4.1 takes the identification of negative name movers as copy suppressors from McDougall et al. and uses it as an interpretive premise.

tranche.reason: The study adopts the prior copy-suppression interpretation to discuss fine-tuning results. Its measurements establish circuit amplification, altered name suppression and total self-repair, without testing the defining copy-suppression mechanism or its causal contribution to compensation.

source_check.notes: Appendix D conflates name movers with copy suppressors, but L9H9 is identified elsewhere as a name mover. The text itself reports 80M parameters; no external correction was applied.

statements.correction: Code link provided. Clean-IOI fine-tuning amplifies negative name-mover mechanisms. Subject Duplication fine-tuning changes their suppression target from IO to S. L9H9 self-repair increases linearly before a phase shift. Dropout and additional backup name movers are proposed explanations requiring further investigation.
statements.problem: The empirical summary matches the text. Reviewed status and the claim that this is the only such study cannot be established from the supplied study. Relevance to V4 and V5 is contextual; the experiments do not isolate copy suppression's contribution to self-repair.
